Subject: Efficiency SKU ask + latency target and quant risk

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the throughput looks great. We’re sizing the economics for a Q2 pilot and have a couple of constraints we need your help making concrete:

- Target p95 generation latency <= 200ms for our typical short-response use case (seq len ~ 128). Can you confirm which SKU(s) and batching configuration hit that bar?
- We need a pricing line that reflects both caching (prefix reuse) and batching credits — our procurement team wants predictable unit pricing if we rely on aggressive batching.
- Quantization: we’re open to int8/4-bit to drop costs, but worried about hallucination/regression. Can you share recommended quant profiles and expected quality delta for our Llama-derivative models?

If you can send a short proposal with options (SLA, price, and technical guardrails) we’ll share with procurement.

Appreciate it — Amit
Amit Mehra
Head of AI Products, Crunchboard
[Attachment: product-requirements.pdf (1 page)]

Subject: Re: Efficiency SKU ask + latency target and quant risk

Hi Amit — thanks, this is helpful. Drafting a concise set of options below and attaching a short SKU sheet + our latest microbenchmarks.

Option A — Low-latency Tier (recommended for p95 <= 200ms)
- Dedicated vCPU-backed cluster with continuous batching set to 16ms window, async KV prefix cache enabled
- Model variant: rwd-llama-2-13B-int8-fast (verified, small quality delta vs fp16)
- Expected p95 (seq 128): 140–190ms depending on burst; sustained throughput 120 qps per GPU
- Price: $0.XXX per 1k tokens (hosted), or 1.2x base commit for Dedicated
- SLA: 99.9% latency SLO for configured routing

Option B — Cost-first Tier
- Shared capacity, batching window 40ms, prefix caching on most-frequent prefixes
- Model variant: rwd-llama-2-13B-quant4 (aggressive quant, good for embeddings-like workloads)
- Expected p95: 220–350ms (not meeting 200ms p95)
- Price: lower per-token tier with credits model for cache hits

Key notes on quantization risk:
- int8: minimal semantic drift for generation prompts we tested; recommend validation suite (we can run your prompt set).
- 4-bit: larger variance; avoid for open-ended generation without evals.
- Canary plan: start on int8 in dedicated pilot, run daily automatic evals vs fp16; roll back to fp16 variant on regression.

Attachments: Crunchboard_Efficiency_SKUs_v3.pdf, quant_benchmarks_jan2028.xlsx

Next steps: I’ll loop in engineering for technical guardrails and a clean pricing table for procurement. Can you share a short prompt set (10–20 prompts) you care most about?

Best,
Soojin Lee
Enterprise AE, Redwood Inference

Quick answers from the infra/quant bench side:

1) SKU/instance: rwd-dedicated-nvl1-v2 (16GB context optimized) with continuous batching (window 12–16ms) + async KV cache will get p95 ~150ms for 13B-int8-fast on our lab trace. Margin varies with realtime variance and network egress – recommend 1.1x capacity cushion for production.

2) Quant profiles (internal names + guidance):
- qint8-fast: our recommended default — mean semantic delta <1.5% on our red-team prompt set, hallucination increase negligible. Good drop-in for most customers.
- qint4-cautious: ~3–7% delta, use only where cost wins matter and prompts are templated/structured.

3) Credits for cache hits: we can provide a cache-credit policy where exact-match prefix reuse gets 60% token credit (i.e., billed at 40% of token cost). Partial-match/kv-hit pricing tier at 80% credit. Implementation: tag requests with cache-hit metadata; billing can consume tagging for reconciliation.

Canary plan (high-level): daily run of 2k validation prompts comparing fp16 baseline; automatic alert if regression >2% on precision metrics or if any prompt fails critical hallucination checks. Rollback window: immediate fallback to fp16 variant for that customer route.

I’ll attach the microbench CSV to the shared drive.

— Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: quant_benchmarks_jan2028.xlsx (spreadsheet)]

Amit — appreciate the quick turn. Below is a compact pricing worked example and the answers to your asks. I’ve attached the formal SKU pdf for procurement.

Worked example (monthly):
- Baseline: 100,000,000 tokens/month (customer estimate)
- Cache hit rate assumption: 30% exact-match prefixes
- Billing rules: cache-hit tokens billed at 40% unit cost; partial cache tokens billed at 80% unit cost

Pricing table (illustrative):
- Dedicated Commit (rwd-dedicated-nvl1-v2): base $X,XXX/month per GPU; per-token charge: $0.008/1k tokens (fp16 baseline)
- qint8-fast discount: applied as 25% reduction to per-token charge when running quant profile
- Effective per-token with 30% cache: = 0.7*(0.008*0.75) + 0.3*(0.008*0.4) ≈ $0.0049/1k tokens (worked math attached)

Shared (hosted) option:
- Per-token: $0.0095/1k tokens with dynamic batching; cache credits applied at invoice reconciliation

Canary cadence: 2-week high-sample canary is fine as a start. We will run the 2k prompt validation daily during the canary (higher sampling intensity) and keep the 2% regression threshold. If stable, move to daily low-intensity checks post-graduation.

Invoice / reconciliation: cache-credit accounting will be visible as line-items — we’ll surface exact-match cache credits and partial-match credits as separate invoice lines tied to route IDs. Procurement will get a CSV export for reconciliation each billing period.

SLO & Remedies: 99.9% p95 latency SLO for the configured route. If missed >0.1% of the month, customer eligible for credit equal to 5% of the affected route’s monthly commit for that billing period (subject to standard SLA terms).

Next steps:
1) Soojin: finalize SKU PDF and a 2-page procurement summary (attached).
2) Amit: send 10–20 prompt samples and desired gradation for canary.
3) Karthik/Dylan: prepare the canary runbook and an ops contact list.

I’ll schedule a 30-min procurement call early next week if that helps.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Enterprise AE, Redwood Inference
